claim: Semantic representations are processed along a posterior-to-anterior gradient reflecting a shift from perceptual to conceptual information.
source: Semantic representations are processed along a posterior-to-anterior gradient reflecting a shift from perceptual (e.g., it has eight legs) to conceptual (e.g., venomous spiders are rare) information.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Borghesani et al., 2016; Peelen and Caramazza, 2012) as indicated in the full manuscript text.

claim: The anterior temporal lobe (ATL) is a critical region for semantic processing.
source: One critical region is the anterior temporal lobe (ATL): patients with semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (svPPA), a clinical syndrome associated with ATL neurodegeneration, manifest a deep loss of semantic knowledge.
evidence: This is supported by the clinical observation that svPPA patients with ATL neurodegeneration show semantic knowledge loss, and is consistent with established neuropsychological literature.

claim: svPPA patients manifest a deep loss of semantic knowledge.
source: One critical region is the anterior temporal lobe (ATL): patients with semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (svPPA), a clinical syndrome associated with ATL neurodegeneration, manifest a deep loss of semantic knowledge.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about svPPA and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: svPPA patients perform semantic tasks by over-recruiting areas implicated in perceptual processing.
source: We test the hypothesis that svPPA patients perform semantic tasks by over-recruiting areas implicated in perceptual processing.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis tested in the study, supported by MEG data showing greater activation in bilateral occipital cortices.

claim: Behavioral performance on the semantic categorization task did not differ between svPPA patients and healthy controls.
source: While behavioral performance did not differ, svPPA patients showed indications of greater activation over bilateral occipital cortices and superior temporal gyrus, and inconsistent engagement of frontal regions.
evidence: This is directly supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1b showing no significant differences in accuracy or reaction times.

claim: svPPA patients showed greater activation over bilateral occipital cortices during semantic categorization.
source: While behavioral performance did not differ, svPPA patients showed indications of greater activation over bilateral occipital cortices and superior temporal gyrus, and inconsistent engagement of frontal regions.
evidence: This is supported by MEG data presented in Figures 2, 3, and Table 2 showing increased synchronization in occipital regions.

claim: svPPA patients showed greater activation over superior temporal gyrus during semantic categorization.
source: While behavioral performance did not differ, svPPA patients showed indications of greater activation over bilateral occipital cortices and superior temporal gyrus, and inconsistent engagement of frontal regions.
evidence: This is supported by MEG data showing increased activity in superior temporal regions as shown in the results section and figures.

claim: svPPA patients showed inconsistent engagement of frontal regions during semantic categorization.
source: While behavioral performance did not differ, svPPA patients showed indications of greater activation over bilateral occipital cortices and superior temporal gyrus, and inconsistent engagement of frontal regions.
evidence: This is supported by MEG data showing variable patterns of frontal activation as detailed in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: The loss of ATL as a critical hub leads to a dysregulated semantic control system.
source: These findings suggest a pervasive reorganization of brain networks in response to ATL neurodegeneration: the loss of this critical hub leads to a dysregulated (semantic) control system, and defective semantic representations are seemingly compensated via enhanced perceptual processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings showing inconsistent frontal engagement, inferred from the data patterns.

claim: Defective semantic representations in svPPA are compensated via enhanced perceptual processing.
source: These findings suggest a pervasive reorganization of brain networks in response to ATL neurodegeneration: the loss of this critical hub leads to a dysregulated (semantic) control system, and defective semantic representations are seemingly compensated via enhanced perceptual processing.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data showing over-recruitment of occipital cortices in svPPA patients.

claim: Visual input analysis requires collecting information on motor-perceptual features such as color, sound, and movement.
source: First, the visual input must be analyzed, collecting information on all possibly relevant motor-perceptual features (e.g., color, sound, movement).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of visual processing.

claim: Extracted features must be merged into a unitary concept to allow proper identification.
source: Then, the extracted features must be merged into a unitary concept to allow proper identification (e.g., it's a rope).
evidence: This is based on established cognitive models of object recognition.

claim: The earliest perceptual processing takes place in the occipital cortex.
source: While the earliest perceptual processing takes place in the occipital cortex, the final stages (i.e., motor programming and execution) entail activation of frontal-parietal structures.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience about visual processing pathways.

claim: Motor programming and execution entail activation of frontal-parietal structures.
source: While the earliest perceptual processing takes place in the occipital cortex, the final stages (i.e., motor programming and execution) entail activation of frontal-parietal structures.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience about motor control.

claim: The transformation from visual input to concept and its semantic categorization has been linked to coordinated activity of multiple neural areas.
source: The critical intermediate steps, involving the transformation from a visual input to a concept (and its semantic categorization as living vs. nonliving, dangerous vs. harmless), have been linked to the coordinated activity of multiple neural areas (Clarke and Tyler, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clarke and Tyler, 2015.

claim: Semantic knowledge is encoded within distributed networks.
source: Functional neuroimaging and neuropsychological research indicate that semantic knowledge is encoded within distributed networks (Huth et al., 2012; Fernandino et al., 2016), with a few key cortical regions acting as critical hubs (Ralph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huth et al., 2012 and Fernandino et al., 2016.

claim: A few key cortical regions act as critical hubs in the semantic network.
source: Functional neuroimaging and neuropsychological research indicate that semantic knowledge is encoded within distributed networks (Huth et al., 2012; Fernandino et al., 2016), with a few key cortical regions acting as critical hubs (Ralph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ralph et al., 2017.

claim: Populations of neurons along the ventral occipito-temporal cortex tune to ecologically relevant categories leading to a nested representational hierarchy of visual information.
source: Prior functional neuroimaging studies suggested that populations of neurons along the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (vOT) tune to ecologically relevant categories leading to a nested representational hierarchy of visual information (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014), where specialized cortical regions respond preferentially to faces (Gauthier et al., 2000; Kanwisher et al., 1997), places (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998), bodies and body parts (Downing et al., 2007; Downing and Kanwisher, 2001), or objects (Lerner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: Specialized cortical regions respond preferentially to faces.
source: Prior functional neuroimaging studies suggested that populations of neurons along the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (vOT) tune to ecologically relevant categories leading to a nested representational hierarchy of visual information (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014), where specialized cortical regions respond preferentially to faces (Gauthier et al., 2000; Kanwisher et al., 1997), places (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998), bodies and body parts (Downing et al., 2007; Downing and Kanwisher, 2001), or objects (Lerner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gauthier et al., 2000 and Kanwisher et al., 1997.

claim: Specialized cortical regions respond preferentially to places.
source: Prior functional neuroimaging studies suggested that populations of neurons along the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (vOT) tune to ecologically relevant categories leading to a nested representational hierarchy of visual information (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014), where specialized cortical regions respond preferentially to faces (Gauthier et al., 2000; Kanwisher et al., 1997), places (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998), bodies and body parts (Downing et al., 2007; Downing and Kanwisher, 2001), or objects (Lerner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998.

claim: Specialized cortical regions respond preferentially to bodies and body parts.
source: Prior functional neuroimaging studies suggested that populations of neurons along the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (vOT) tune to ecologically relevant categories leading to a nested representational hierarchy of visual information (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014), where specialized cortical regions respond preferentially to faces (Gauthier et al., 2000; Kanwisher et al., 1997), places (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998), bodies and body parts (Downing et al., 2007; Downing and Kanwisher, 2001), or objects (Lerner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Downing et al., 2007 and Downing and Kanwisher, 2001.

claim: Specialized cortical regions respond preferentially to objects.
source: Prior functional neuroimaging studies suggested that populations of neurons along the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (vOT) tune to ecologically relevant categories leading to a nested representational hierarchy of visual information (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014), where specialized cortical regions respond preferentially to faces (Gauthier et al., 2000; Kanwisher et al., 1997), places (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998), bodies and body parts (Downing et al., 2007; Downing and Kanwisher, 2001), or objects (Lerner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lerner et al., 2001.

claim: Living stimuli recruit lateral portions of ventral occipito-temporal cortex.
source: Living stimuli appear to recruit lateral portions of vOT, while nonliving stimuli are highlighted in medial regions (Martin and Chao, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin and Chao, 2001.

claim: Nonliving stimuli are highlighted in medial regions of ventral occipito-temporal cortex.
source: Living stimuli appear to recruit lateral portions of vOT, while nonliving stimuli are highlighted in medial regions (Martin and Chao, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin and Chao, 2001.

claim: Agency and visual categorizability are organizing principles responsible for the representational organization of ventral occipito-temporal areas.
source: Multiple organizing principles appear to be responsible for the representational organization of these areas, including agency and visual categorizability (Thorat et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thorat et al., 2019.

claim: Semantic processing is supported by the interaction of a perceptual representational system arising along the occipito-temporal pathway, a semantic representational system confined to the ATL, and a semantic control system supported by fronto-parietal cortices.
source: Neuropsychological findings corroborate the idea of a distributed yet specialized organization of semantic processing in the brain, supported by the interaction of a perceptual representational system arising along the occipito-temporal pathway, a semantic representational system confined to the anterior temporal lobe (ATL), and a semantic control system supported by fronto-parietal cortices (Ralph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ralph et al., 2017 and represents an established neuropsychological model.

claim: Focal lesions in the occipito-temporal pathway are associated with selective impairment for living items and spared performance on nonliving ones.
source: For instance, focal lesions in the occipito-temporal pathway are associated with selective impairment for living items and spared performance on nonliving ones (Blundo et al., 2006; Caramazza and Shelton, 1998; Laiacona et al., 2003; Pietrini et al., 1988; Sartori et al., 1993; Warrington and Shallice, 1984) as well as the opposite pattern (Laiacona and Capitani, 2001; Sacchett and Humphreys, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to neuropsychological case studies.

claim: Focal lesions in the occipito-temporal pathway can produce the opposite pattern of selective impairment for nonliving items.
source: For instance, focal lesions in the occipito-temporal pathway are associated with selective impairment for living items and spared performance on nonliving ones (Blundo et al., 2006; Caramazza and Shelton, 1998; Laiacona et al., 2003; Pietrini et al., 1988; Sartori et al., 1993; Warrington and Shallice, 1984) as well as the opposite pattern (Laiacona and Capitani, 2001; Sacchett and Humphreys, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Laiacona and Capitani, 2001 and Sacchett and Humphreys, 1992.

claim: Acute brain damage to prefrontal or temporoparietal cortices in the semantic control system has been linked with semantic aphasia.
source: Moreover, acute brain damage to prefrontal or temporoparietal cortices in the semantic control system has been linked with semantic aphasia, a clinical syndrome characterized by deficits in tasks requiring manipulations of semantic knowledge (Jefferies and Lambon Ralph, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jefferies and Lambon Ralph, 2006.

claim: Semantic aphasia is characterized by deficits in tasks requiring manipulations of semantic knowledge.
source: Moreover, acute brain damage to prefrontal or temporoparietal cortices in the semantic control system has been linked with semantic aphasia, a clinical syndrome characterized by deficits in tasks requiring manipulations of semantic knowledge (Jefferies and Lambon Ralph, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jefferies and Lambon Ralph, 2006.

claim: svPPA is associated with ATL neurodegeneration as confirmed by gray matter atrophy.
source: This rare syndrome is associated with ATL neurodegeneration as confirmed by the observation of gray matter atrophy (Collins et al., 2016), white matter alterations (Galantucci et al., 2011), and hypometabolism (Diehl et al., 2004), as well as neuropathological findings (Hodges and Patterson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2016.

claim: svPPA is associated with white matter alterations.
source: This rare syndrome is associated with ATL neurodegeneration as confirmed by the observation of gray matter atrophy (Collins et al., 2016), white matter alterations (Galantucci et al., 2011), and hypometabolism (Diehl et al., 2004), as well as neuropathological findings (Hodges and Patterson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galantucci et al., 2011.

claim: svPPA is associated with hypometabolism.
source: This rare syndrome is associated with ATL neurodegeneration as confirmed by the observation of gray matter atrophy (Collins et al., 2016), white matter alterations (Galantucci et al., 2011), and hypometabolism (Diehl et al., 2004), as well as neuropathological findings (Hodges and Patterson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Diehl et al., 2004.

claim: Patients with svPPA present with single-word comprehension deficits, surface dyslexia, and impaired object knowledge.
source: Patients with svPPA present with an array of impairments (e.g., single-word comprehension deficits, surface dyslexia, impaired object knowledge) that can be traced back to a generalized loss of semantic knowledge, often affecting all stimuli modalities and all semantic categories (Hodges and Patterson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hodges and Patterson, 2007 and represents established clinical knowledge.

claim: svPPA impairments can be traced back to a generalized loss of semantic knowledge, often affecting all stimuli modalities and all semantic categories.
source: Patients with svPPA present with an array of impairments (e.g., single-word comprehension deficits, surface dyslexia, impaired object knowledge) that can be traced back to a generalized loss of semantic knowledge, often affecting all stimuli modalities and all semantic categories (Hodges and Patterson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hodges and Patterson, 2007.

claim: Executive functions and perceptual abilities are relatively preserved in svPPA patients.
source: Conversely, executive functions and perceptual abilities are relatively preserved.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about svPPA.

claim: svPPA patients provide crucial neuropsychological evidence of the role played by the ATL in the storage of semantic representations.
source: Hence, these patients provide crucial neuropsychological evidence of the role played by the ATL in the storage of semantic representations, and can be leveraged to investigate the breakdown of the semantic system and the resulting compensatory mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical profile of svPPA and established neuropsychological theory.

claim: Task-based imaging in patients is hampered by specific difficulties such as patients' compliance.
source: However, task-based imaging in patients is hampered by specific difficulties (e.g., patients' compliance) and limitations (e.g., performance is not matched and error signals can act as confounds) (Price et al., 2006; Wilson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Price et al., 2006 and Wilson et al., 2018.

claim: Performance mismatch and error signals can act as confounds in patient imaging studies.
source: However, task-based imaging in patients is hampered by specific difficulties (e.g., patients' compliance) and limitations (e.g., performance is not matched and error signals can act as confounds) (Price et al., 2006; Wilson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Price et al., 2006 and Wilson et al., 2018.

claim: Residual semantic abilities in svPPA come from recruitment of homologous and perilesional temporal regions.
source: Previous findings suggest that residual semantic abilities come from the recruitment of homologous and perilesional temporal regions, as well as increased functional demands on the semantic control system, that is, parietal/frontal regions (Maguire et al., 2010; Mummery et al., 1999; Pineault et al., 2019; Viard et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior imaging studies.

claim: Residual semantic abilities in svPPA involve increased functional demands on the semantic control system (parietal/frontal regions).
source: Previous findings suggest that residual semantic abilities come from the recruitment of homologous and perilesional temporal regions, as well as increased functional demands on the semantic control system, that is, parietal/frontal regions (Maguire et al., 2010; Mummery et al., 1999; Pineault et al., 2019; Viard et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior imaging studies.

claim: MEG imaging has proven useful in detecting syndrome-specific network-level abnormalities in neurodegenerative patients.
source: Recently, magnetoencephalographic (MEG) imaging has proven useful in detecting syndrome-specific network-level abnormalities (Ranasinghe et al., 2017; Sami et al., 2018) as well as task-related functional alterations (Kielar et al., 2018) in neurodegenerative patients.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ranasinghe et al., 2017 and Sami et al., 2018.

claim: MEG imaging has proven useful in detecting task-related functional alterations in neurodegenerative patients.
source: Recently, magnetoencephalographic (MEG) imaging has proven useful in detecting syndrome-specific network-level abnormalities (Ranasinghe et al., 2017; Sami et al., 2018) as well as task-related functional alterations (Kielar et al., 2018) in neurodegenerative patients.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kielar et al., 2018.

claim: Imperfect behavioral compensation can be achieved via reorganization of dynamic activity in the brain.
source: Critically, it has been suggested that imperfect behavioral compensation can be achieved via reorganization of the dynamic activity in the brain (Borghesani et al., 2020): owing to their damage to the ventral, lexico-semantic reading route, svPPA patients appear to over-recruit the dorsal, sublexical/phonological pathway to read not only pseudowords, but also irregular ones.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Borghesani et al., 2020.

claim: svPPA patients over-recruit the dorsal, sublexical/phonological pathway to read both pseudowords and irregular words.
source: Critically, it has been suggested that imperfect behavioral compensation can be achieved via reorganization of the dynamic activity in the brain (Borghesani et al., 2020): owing to their damage to the ventral, lexico-semantic reading route, svPPA patients appear to over-recruit the dorsal, sublexical/phonological pathway to read not only pseudowords, but also irregular ones.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Borghesani et al., 2020.

claim: There were no statistically significant effects of diagnosis, category, or their interaction in percentage accuracy during the semantic categorization task.
source: There were no statistically significant effects of diagnosis, category, nor their interaction neither in percentage accuracy (healthy controls [HC]: living: 97.1 ± 6.6, nonliving: 96.8 ± 6.6; svPPA: living: 91.5 ± 6.2, nonliving: 95.9 ± 8.1) nor in reaction times (HC: living: 826.3 ± 112.5, nonliving: 856.9 ± 104.4; svPPA: living: 869.8 ± 179.8, nonliving: 911.1 ± 194.45).
evidence: This is directly supported by the behavioral data analysis and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: There were no statistically significant effects of diagnosis, category, or their interaction in reaction times during the semantic categorization task.
source: There were no statistically significant effects of diagnosis, category, nor their interaction neither in percentage accuracy (healthy controls [HC]: living: 97.1 ± 6.6, nonliving: 96.8 ± 6.6; svPPA: living: 91.5 ± 6.2, nonliving: 95.9 ± 8.1) nor in reaction times (HC: living: 826.3 ± 112.5, nonliving: 856.9 ± 104.4; svPPA: living: 869.8 ± 179.8, nonliving: 911.1 ± 194.45).
evidence: This is directly supported by the behavioral data analysis and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: svPPA patients can perform the semantic categorization task as proficiently as healthy elders.
source: Overall, these results indicate that svPPA patients can perform the task as proficiently as healthy elders, an expected finding due to the relatively shallow semantic processing requirements and simple stimuli used in the task (see Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data showing no significant differences in performance.

claim: The preserved performance in svPPA is due to the relatively shallow semantic processing requirements and simple stimuli used in the task.
source: Overall, these results indicate that svPPA patients can perform the task as proficiently as healthy elders, an expected finding due to the relatively shallow semantic processing requirements and simple stimuli used in the task (see Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an inference based on task design and behavioral results.

claim: svPPA patients present atrophy in the ATL, involving the temporal pole, the inferior and middle temporal gyrus.
source: Patients present atrophy in the ATL, involving the temporal pole, the inferior and middle temporal gyrus.
evidence: This is supported by VBM analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The pattern of neurodegeneration in svPPA is bilateral yet strongly left-lateralized.
source: This pattern of neurodegeneration, bilateral yet strongly left-lateralized, is consistent with their clinical diagnosis and overall neuropsychological profile (see Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the VBM results shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The atrophy pattern in svPPA is consistent with their clinical diagnosis and overall neuropsychological profile.
source: This pattern of neurodegeneration, bilateral yet strongly left-lateralized, is consistent with their clinical diagnosis and overall neuropsychological profile (see Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of VBM results with clinical data in Table 1.

claim: Following presentation of images, both cohorts showed posterior-to-anterior progression of functional activation across all five frequency bands.
source: In brief, following presentation of the images both cohorts showed posterior-to-anterior progression of functional activation across all five frequency bands.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the high-gamma band, bilateral increases in synchronous power were observed starting in the occipital cortex and progressively extending to temporal, parietal, and frontal regions.
source: In the high-gamma band (63–117 Hz, see Figure 2a), we observed bilateral increases in synchronous power starting in the occipital cortex and progressively extending to temporal, parietal, and frontal regions.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: In the low-gamma band, subjects show heightened synchronization over bilateral occipital cortices, evident early in the svPPA group and only later in HC.
source: In the low-gamma band (30–55 Hz, see Figure 2b), subjects show heightened synchronization over bilateral occipital cortices, evident early in the svPPA group and only later in HC.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Both groups showed reductions in low-gamma activity over frontal cortices starting mid-trial.
source: Moreover, both groups showed reductions in activity over frontal cortices starting mid-trial.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Beta and alpha band activity revealed significant reductions in synchronous activity for both groups, extending from bilateral occipital cortices to temporal and parietal lobes.
source: A similar progression of beta (12–30 Hz, see Figure 2c) and alpha (8–12 Hz, see Figure 2d) band activity revealed significant reductions in synchronous activity for both groups, extending from bilateral occipital cortices to temporal and parietal lobes, and involving progressively larger areas in precentral and superior frontal gyrus.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data shown in Figures 2c and 2d.

claim: A focus of increased alpha synchrony in anterior cingulate regions, mid-trial, is evident in both groups.
source: A focus of increased alpha synchrony in anterior cingulate regions, mid-trial, is evident in both groups.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Induced theta band activity revealed progressive increases in synchronous activity over bilateral occipital cortices.
source: Finally, induced theta band (3–7 Hz, see Figure 2e) activity revealed progressive increases in synchronous activity over bilateral occipital cortices, a similarly progressive pattern of increased synchronization within frontal regions at an onset window after that of occipital regions, and progressively reduced theta activity relative to baseline levels over parietal and temporal lobes.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Theta band activity showed a progressive pattern of increased synchronization within frontal regions at an onset window after that of occipital regions.
source: Finally, induced theta band (3–7 Hz, see Figure 2e) activity revealed progressive increases in synchronous activity over bilateral occipital cortices, a similarly progressive pattern of increased synchronization within frontal regions at an onset window after that of occipital regions, and progressively reduced theta activity relative to baseline levels over parietal and temporal lobes.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Theta band activity showed progressively reduced activity relative to baseline levels over parietal and temporal lobes.
source: Finally, induced theta band (3–7 Hz, see Figure 2e) activity revealed progressive increases in synchronous activity over bilateral occipital cortices, a similarly progressive pattern of increased synchronization within frontal regions at an onset window after that of occipital regions, and progressively reduced theta activity relative to baseline levels over parietal and temporal lobes.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Stimulus-locked task-induced changes indicate the expected pattern of visual processing followed by motor response preparation in both cohorts and across all frequency bands.
source: Taken together, these stimulus-locked task-induced changes indicate, in both cohorts and across all frequency bands, the expected pattern of visual processing followed by motor response preparation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG data patterns shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the high-gamma band, svPPA patients showed significantly higher synchronization over left superior temporal cortices at both early and late time points relative to controls.
source: In the high-gamma band, we detected significantly higher synchronization in svPPA patients, relative to controls, over left superior temporal (at both early and late time points) and right frontal (at late time points) cortices (see Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the between-group MEG analysis shown in Figure 3a and Table 2.

claim: In the high-gamma band, svPPA patients showed significantly higher synchronization over right frontal cortices at late time points relative to controls.
source: In the high-gamma band, we detected significantly higher synchronization in svPPA patients, relative to controls, over left superior temporal (at both early and late time points) and right frontal (at late time points) cortices (see Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the between-group MEG analysis shown in Figure 3a and Table 2.

claim: In the low-gamma band, an extensive spatiotemporal cluster over bilateral occipital cortices showed significantly higher synchronized activity in svPPA patients relative to controls.
source: In the low-gamma band, we observed an extensive spatiotemporal cluster over bilateral occipital cortices with significantly higher synchronized activity in svPPA patients relative to controls.
evidence: This is supported by the between-group MEG analysis shown in Figure 3b and Table 2.

claim: Small clusters of gamma activity in medial frontal cortices at ~300 ms showed relatively more desynchronization in HC than svPPA, resulting in increased gamma synchrony in the svPPA group.
source: Similarly, small clusters of gamma activity, relatively more desynchronized in HC than svPPA, resulted in an increased gamma synchrony in medial frontal cortices at ~300 ms for the svPPA group (see Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by the between-group MEG analysis shown in Figure 3b and Table 2.

claim: Results at high frequencies (30–117 Hz) suggest higher activity in svPPA over bilateral occipital and left superior temporal cortices throughout the trial, and right frontal cortices at late time points.
source: Overall, the results at high frequencies (30–117 Hz) suggest thus higher activity in svPPA over bilateral occipital and left superior temporal cortices throughout the trial, and right frontal cortices at late time points.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the high-frequency MEG data.

claim: In beta band, svPPA patients showed more desynchronization over the left superior temporal gyrus at ~300 ms.
source: Between-group contrast in beta band revealed, in svPPA patients, more desynchronization (i.e., more beta suppression) over the left superior temporal gyrus at ~300 ms, while simultaneously displaying less desynchronization in a right middle-frontal cluster (see Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by the between-group MEG analysis shown in Figure 3c and Table 2.

claim: In beta band, svPPA patients showed less desynchronization in a right middle-frontal cluster at ~300 ms.
source: Between-group contrast in beta band revealed, in svPPA patients, more desynchronization (i.e., more beta suppression) over the left superior temporal gyrus at ~300 ms, while simultaneously displaying less desynchronization in a right middle-frontal cluster (see Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by the between-group MEG analysis shown in Figure 3c and Table 2.

claim: In the alpha band, svPPA patients showed less desynchronization over left middle temporal gyrus at ~300 ms.
source: In the alpha band, svPPA patients showed less desynchronization over left middle temporal gyrus at ~300 ms as well as in later clusters in the right precentral gyrus, left anterior cingulate, and left parahippocampal gyrus (see Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by the between-group MEG analysis shown in Figure 3d and Table 2.

claim: In the alpha band, svPPA patients showed less desynchronization in later clusters in the right precentral gyrus, left anterior cingulate, and left parahippocampal gyrus.
source: In the alpha band, svPPA patients showed less desynchronization over left middle temporal gyrus at ~300 ms as well as in later clusters in the right precentral gyrus, left anterior cingulate, and left parahippocampal gyrus (see Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by the between-group MEG analysis shown in Figure 3d and Table 2.

claim: In the theta band, significant differences over the left occipital cortex occurred at both early (~100 ms) and late (~500 ms) time points indicating higher synchronization in svPPA patients compared to HC.
source: Finally, in the theta band, significant differences over the left occipital cortex occurred at both early (~100 ms) and late (~500 ms) time points indicating higher synchronization in svPPA patients compared to HC, while the opposite pattern (i.e., higher activity for HC) is observed in a right frontal cluster at ~300 ms (see Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by the between-group MEG analysis shown in Figure 3e and Table 2.

claim: In the theta band, higher activity for HC compared to svPPA is observed in a right frontal cluster at ~300 ms.
source: Finally, in the theta band, significant differences over the left occipital cortex occurred at both early (~100 ms) and late (~500 ms) time points indicating higher synchronization in svPPA patients compared to HC, while the opposite pattern (i.e., higher activity for HC) is observed in a right frontal cluster at ~300 ms (see Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by the between-group MEG analysis shown in Figure 3e and Table 2.

claim: Results at low frequencies (3–30 Hz) suggest higher activity in svPPA over bilateral occipital and left superior temporal cortices, while indicating less activity in left middle temporal and right frontal regions.
source: Overall, the results at low frequencies (3–30 Hz) suggest thus higher activity in svPPA over bilateral occipital and left superior temporal cortices, while indicating less activity in left middle temporal and right frontal regions.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the low-frequency MEG data.

claim: svPPA patients performed the semantic categorization tasks by over-recruiting bilateral occipital cortices and left superior temporal gyrus, while showing less reliance on left middle temporal regions and inconsistent engagement of frontal ones.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that svPPA patients performed the semantic categorization tasks by over-recruiting bilateral occipital cortices and left superior temporal gyrus, while showing less reliance on left middle temporal regions and inconsistent engagement of frontal ones.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of all the MEG findings.

claim: The main difference between svPPA patients and HC is heightened low-gamma activity over the occipital region.
source: It appears clear that the main difference between svPPA patients and HC is heightened low-gamma activity over the occipital region.
evidence: This is supported by the ROI analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The heightened low-gamma activity difference in svPPA is evident around 100 ms post stimuli onset, peaks around 200 ms, and continues throughout the whole trial.
source: Such difference is evident around 100 ms post stimuli onset, peaks around 200 ms, and continues throughout the whole.
evidence: This is supported by the ROI analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The observed whole brain differences cannot be explained as mere temporal shift or spreading.
source: These findings rule out an explanation of the observed whole brain differences as mere temporal shift or spreading, while highlighting the spatial specificity of the main results.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ROI analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: A broad and sustained increase in low-gamma band power is observed in svPPA patients and not in HC.
source: Critically, a broad and sustained increase in low-gamma band power is observed in svPPA patients and not in HC, with no traces of cross-spectral leakage between beta and low gamma, or low and high gamma.
evidence: This is supported by the time-frequency analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: There are no traces of cross-spectral leakage between beta and low gamma, or low and high gamma in the MEG data.
source: Critically, a broad and sustained increase in low-gamma band power is observed in svPPA patients and not in HC, with no traces of cross-spectral leakage between beta and low gamma, or low and high gamma.
evidence: This is supported by the time-frequency analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The observed effects cannot be interpreted in terms of frequency shift or spread.
source: These findings rule out a possible interpretation of the observed effects in terms of frequency shift or spread, highlighting the spectral specificity of the main results.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time-frequency analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: This is the first study investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics of semantic categorization of visual stimuli in a cohort of svPPA patients.
source: This is the first study investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics of semantic categorization of visual stimuli in a cohort of svPPA patients.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: svPPA patients recruit additional perilesional and distal cortical regions to achieve normal performance on a shallow semantic task.
source: We provide compelling evidence that, burdened with ATL damage, svPPA patients recruit additional perilesional and distal cortical regions to achieve normal performance on a shallow semantic task.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by the MEG and behavioral data.

claim: svPPA patients showed greater activation over bilateral occipital cortices and superior temporal gyrus compared to healthy age-matched controls.
source: As compared to healthy age-matched controls, svPPA patients showed greater activation over bilateral occipital cortices and superior temporal gyrus, indicating over-reliance on perceptual processing and spared dorsal language networks.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data analysis.

claim: Greater activation in occipital and superior temporal regions in svPPA indicates over-reliance on perceptual processing and spared dorsal language networks.
source: As compared to healthy age-matched controls, svPPA patients showed greater activation over bilateral occipital cortices and superior temporal gyrus, indicating over-reliance on perceptual processing and spared dorsal language networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings.

claim: Inconsistent engagement of frontal areas in svPPA suggests less efficient control responses.
source: Conversely, they showed inconsistent engagement of frontal regions, suggesting less efficient control responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings showing variable frontal activation patterns.

claim: The findings have important implications for current neurocognitive models of the language systems.
source: These findings have important implications both for current neurocognitive models of the language systems and on the utility of MEG imaging in clinical populations.
evidence: This is a claim about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: The findings have important implications for the utility of MEG imaging in clinical populations.
source: These findings have important implications both for current neurocognitive models of the language systems and on the utility of MEG imaging in clinical populations.
evidence: This is a claim about the methodological significance of the findings.

claim: The results speak to the distributed and dynamic organization of the semantic system, where semantic representations are supported by occipito-temporal cortices and semantic control by fronto-parietal areas.
source: These results speak to the distributed and dynamic organization of the semantic system, where semantic representations are supported by occipito-temporal cortices and semantic control by fronto-parietal areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of existing neurocognitive models.

claim: Normal performance can be achieved via altered neural dynamics in neurological patients.
source: Second, the observation that normal performance can be achieved via altered neural dynamics elucidates the neurocognitive mechanisms that support compensation in neurological patients.
evidence: This is supported by the finding that svPPA patients perform normally despite different neural activation patterns.

claim: Network-driven neurodegeneration leads to the reorganization of the interplay of various cortical regions.
source: Specifically, we contribute to the body of literature illustrating how network-driven neurodegeneration leads to the reorganization of the interplay of various cortical regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of neurodegeneration research.

claim: svPPA patients can achieve normal performance in a shallow semantic task by over-relying on perilesional language-related regions (STG), as well as on distal visual (occipital) and executive (frontal) networks.
source: Our key finding is that svPPA patients can achieve normal performance in a shallow semantic task by over-relying on perilesional language-related regions (STG), as well as on distal visual (occipital) and executive (frontal) networks.
evidence: This is the main finding supported by both behavioral and MEG data.

claim: At frequencies spanning low and high gamma bands, svPPA patients show increased activity in occipital and superior temporal cortices relative to healthy counterparts.
source: At frequencies spanning low and high gamma bands, svPPA patients show increased activity in occipital and superior temporal cortices relative to their healthy counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data analysis in the gamma frequency ranges.

claim: Gamma oscillations have been associated with local computations.
source: Gamma oscillations have been associated with local computations (Donner and Siegel, 2011), promoting binding and selective long-range communication (Hagoort et al., 2004; Fries, 2015), including merging of multimodal semantic information (van Ackeren et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on gamma oscillations.

claim: Gamma oscillations promote binding and selective long-range communication.
source: Gamma oscillations have been associated with local computations (Donner and Siegel, 2011), promoting binding and selective long-range communication (Hagoort et al., 2004; Fries, 2015), including merging of multimodal semantic information (van Ackeren et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hagoort et al., 2004 and Fries, 2015.

claim: Gamma oscillations are involved in merging of multimodal semantic information.
source: Gamma oscillations have been associated with local computations (Donner and Siegel, 2011), promoting binding and selective long-range communication (Hagoort et al., 2004; Fries, 2015), including merging of multimodal semantic information (van Ackeren et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Ackeren et al., 2014.

claim: Theta oscillations have been associated with operations over distributed networks, such as those required for lexico-semantic retrieval.
source: Theta oscillations have generally been associated with operations over distributed networks, such as those required for lexico-semantic retrieval (Bastiaansen et al., 2005; Bastiaansen et al., 2008; Kielar et al., 2015), integration of unimodal semantic features (van Ackeren et al., 2014), and facilitating phase-specific coupling of selective communication between regions (Fries, 2015; Canolty et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bastiaansen et al., 2005, 2008 and Kielar et al., 2015.

claim: Theta oscillations are involved in integration of unimodal semantic features.
source: Theta oscillations have generally been associated with operations over distributed networks, such as those required for lexico-semantic retrieval (Bastiaansen et al., 2005; Bastiaansen et al., 2008; Kielar et al., 2015), integration of unimodal semantic features (van Ackeren et al., 2014), and facilitating phase-specific coupling of selective communication between regions (Fries, 2015; Canolty et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Ackeren et al., 2014.

claim: Theta oscillations facilitate phase-specific coupling of selective communication between regions.
source: Theta oscillations have generally been associated with operations over distributed networks, such as those required for lexico-semantic retrieval (Bastiaansen et al., 2005; Bastiaansen et al., 2008; Kielar et al., 2015), integration of unimodal semantic features (van Ackeren et al., 2014), and facilitating phase-specific coupling of selective communication between regions (Fries, 2015; Canolty et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fries, 2015 and Canolty et al., 2006.

claim: In svPPA patients, compensation for faulty semantic representations relies primarily on local and distributed computations in networks associated with perceptual processing.
source: Therefore, in our patients, compensation for faulty semantic representations seems to rely primarily on local and distributed computations in networks associated with perceptual processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings in the context of oscillatory function.

claim: The semantic task can be performed by focusing on a few key, distinctive, motor-perceptual features.
source: In principle, the semantic task employed in the current study (i.e., identifying a visually presented object as either a living or nonliving) can be performed by focusing on a few key, distinctive, motor-perceptual features: if it has eyes and teeth, it is a living being.
evidence: This is an inference about the task demands based on the task design.

claim: Object identification and naming require the integration of multiple motor perceptual as well as conceptual features.
source: Further processing steps, such as would be required for an object identification and naming (i.e., accessing the appropriate lexical label), require the integration of multiple motor perceptual as well as conceptual features (Borghesani and Piazza, 2017): a python is a nonvenomous snake that kills by constriction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Borghesani and Piazza, 2017 and represents established knowledge.

claim: HC can recognize and likely inevitably mentally name each item in the task.
source: Combining the behavioral data collected during the recordings and outside and the scanner (see Boston Naming Task performance, Table 1), it appears clear that HC can recognize (and likely inevitably mentally name) each item, while svPPA patients can only provide the categorical label.
evidence: This is an inference based on behavioral performance data in Table 1.

claim: svPPA patients can only provide the categorical label for items in the task.
source: Combining the behavioral data collected during the recordings and outside and the scanner (see Boston Naming Task performance, Table 1), it appears clear that HC can recognize (and likely inevitably mentally name) each item, while svPPA patients can only provide the categorical label.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data showing impaired naming but preserved categorization.

claim: Patient data is critical in characterizing the division of labor between the distributed set of cortical regions involved in semantic processing.
source: Patient data is thus critical in characterizing the division of labor between the distributed set of cortical regions involved in semantic processing.
evidence: This is a claim about the value of patient studies for understanding brain function.

claim: ATL damage hampers operation of the semantic representation system by shattering conceptual components and forcing over-reliance on perceptual features coded in posterior cortices.
source: Our findings strongly suggest that ATL damage hampers operation of the semantic representation system, by shattering their conceptual components and thus forcing over-reliance on perceptual features coded in posterior cortices.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by the MEG data.

claim: The ability to merge perceptual features into semantic concepts relies on the integrity of the ATL.
source: For instance, it has been shown that the ability to merge perceptual features into semantic concepts relies on the integrity of the ATL (Hoffman et al., 2014), and that ATL damage promotes reliance on perceptual similarities over conceptual ones (Lambon Ralph et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoffman et al., 2014.

claim: ATL damage promotes reliance on perceptual similarities over conceptual ones.
source: For instance, it has been shown that the ability to merge perceptual features into semantic concepts relies on the integrity of the ATL (Hoffman et al., 2014), and that ATL damage promotes reliance on perceptual similarities over conceptual ones (Lambon Ralph et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lambon Ralph et al., 2010.

claim: The more motor-perceptual information is associated with a given concept, the more resilient it is to damage.
source: Moreover, it appears that the more motor-perceptual information is associated with a given concept, the more resilient it is to damage, an advantage that is lost once the disease progresses from ATL to posterior ventral temporal regions (Hoffman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoffman et al., 2012.

claim: The advantage of motor-perceptual information for concept resilience is lost once the disease progresses from ATL to posterior ventral temporal regions.
source: Moreover, it appears that the more motor-perceptual information is associated with a given concept, the more resilient it is to damage, an advantage that is lost once the disease progresses from ATL to posterior ventral temporal regions (Hoffman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoffman et al., 2012.

claim: Compared to HC, svPPA patients appear to have less activation in the left middle temporal gyrus.
source: Compared to HC, svPPA patients appear to have less activation in the left middle temporal gyrus and to inconsistently engage frontal regions, suggesting that increased demands to the semantic control systems are met by inefficient responses in prefrontal and superior frontal cortices.
evidence: This is supported by the MEG data analysis.

claim: Increased demands to the semantic control systems in svPPA are met by inefficient responses in prefrontal and superior frontal cortices.
source: Compared to HC, svPPA patients appear to have less activation in the left middle temporal gyrus and to inconsistently engage frontal regions, suggesting that increased demands to the semantic control systems are met by inefficient responses in prefrontal and superior frontal cortices.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings showing inconsistent frontal engagement.

claim: In svPPA, an enhanced late high-frequency (local neural) response occurs compared to an earlier and lower frequency (long-range connection) response in controls.
source: Comparing the two cohorts across frequency bands, it appears that an enhanced late high-frequency (local neural) response occurs in svPPA, vs. an earlier and lower frequency (long-range connection) response in controls.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG data comparing frequency and timing patterns between groups.

claim: An initial inefficient response in the semantic cognitive control network centered on frontal areas in svPPA leads to a later higher reliance on local activity for semantic cognitive control and decision-making processes.
source: One speculation for this pattern is that in svPPA, an initial inefficient response in the (semantic) cognitive control network centered on frontal areas leads to a later higher reliance on local activity for (semantic) cognitive control and decision-making processes.
evidence: This is explicitly labeled as speculation based on the observed patterns.

claim: Object recognition in visual areas is facilitated by prior knowledge received via feedback projections from both frontal and anterior temporal cortices.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that object recognition in visual areas is facilitated by prior knowledge (Bannert and Bartels, 2013) received via feedback projections from both frontal (Bar et al., 2006) and anterior temporal (Coutanche and Thompson-Schill, 2015) cortices.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bannert and Bartels, 2013; Bar et al., 2006; and Coutanche and Thompson-Schill, 2015.

claim: Higher demands for feature integration entail more recurrent activity between fusiform and ATL.
source: Moreover, it has been observed that higher demands for feature integration entail more recurrent activity between fusiform and ATL (Clarke et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clarke et al., 2011.

claim: The study provides a direct contrast between subjects in which both frontal and ATL feedback inputs are preserved (HC), and those in which ATL neurodegeneration forces reliance exclusively on frontal inputs.
source: Our study provides a direct contrast between subjects in which both frontal and ATL feedback inputs are preserved (HC), and those in which ATL neurodegeneration forces reliance exclusively on frontal inputs.
evidence: This is a claim about the unique contribution of the study design.

claim: The observed temporal dynamics are not compatible with a strictly feedforward model of visual stimuli processing.
source: Interestingly, the observed temporal dynamics (with the detection of early frontal involvement) are not compatible with a strictly feedforward model of visual stimuli processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal patterns observed in the MEG data.

claim: Recurrent neural models are needed to explain the representational transformations supporting visual information processing.
source: This is in line with recent evidence that recurrent neural models are needed to explain the representational transformations supporting visual information processing (Gwilliams and King, 2019; Kietzmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gwilliams and King, 2019 and Kietzmann et al., 2019.

claim: The conversion from percept to concept is supported by recurrent loops over fronto-parietal and occipito-temporal regions which have been implicated in semantic control and semantic representations.
source: Thus, taken together, our findings corroborate the idea that the conversion from percept to concept is supported by recurrent loops over fronto-parietal and occipito-temporal regions which have been implicated in, respectively, semantic control and semantic representations (Chiou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citation to Chiou et al., 2018.

claim: Neurodegeneration leads to the dynamic reorganization of distributed networks.
source: Our findings corroborate the idea that neurodegeneration leads to the dynamic reorganization of distributed networks (Agosta et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2013), and that task-based MEG imaging can be instrumental in deepening our understanding of the resulting alterations (Borghesani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Agosta et al., 2014 and Guo et al., 2013.

claim: Task-based MEG imaging can be instrumental in deepening our understanding of alterations resulting from neurodegeneration.
source: Our findings corroborate the idea that neurodegeneration leads to the dynamic reorganization of distributed networks (Agosta et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2013), and that task-based MEG imaging can be instrumental in deepening our understanding of the resulting alterations (Borghesani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Borghesani et al., 2020 and the current study's findings.

claim: Functional changes are known to precede structural ones in neurodegeneration.
source: Ultimately, these efforts will pave the way toward treatment options, as well as better early diagnostic markers as functional changes are known to precede structural ones (Bonakdarpour et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bonakdarpour et al., 2017.

claim: The origin of svPPA patients' difficulties during semantic categorization tasks are linked to degraded feature knowledge rather than to a deficit of executive processes.
source: For instance, our results support previous neuropsychological evidence suggesting that the origin of svPPA patients' difficulties during semantic categorization tasks are linked to degraded feature knowledge rather than, as it happens in other FTDs (fronto-temporal dementias), to a deficit of executive processes (Koenig et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koenig et al., 2006 and the current study's findings.

claim: Heightened activity has been reported in periatrophic left anterior superior temporal gyrus as well as more distant left premotor cortex, and right ATL in svPPA patients.
source: Heightened activity has been reported in periatrophic left anterior superior temporal gyrus as well as more distant left premotor cortex, and right ATL (Mummery et al., 1999; Pineault et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mummery et al., 1999 and Pineault et al., 2019.

claim: Individual subject analyses have indicated that svPPA patients might attempt different compensatory strategies, which may vary in terms of efficiency and would rely on the recruitment of different cortical networks.
source: Individual subject analyses have indicated that patients might attempt different compensatory strategies, which may vary in terms of efficiency and, crucially, would rely on the recruitment of different cortical networks (Viard et al., 2013; Viard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Viard et al., 2013 and 2014.

claim: Studies on reading have associated svPPA patients' imperfect compensation of the semantic deficit (leading to regularization errors) with over-reliance on parietal regions subserving sublexical processes.
source: For instance, studies on reading have associated svPPA patients' imperfect compensation of the semantic deficit (leading to regularization errors) with over-reliance on parietal regions subserving sublexical processes (Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2009.

claim: In svPPA patients, decreased connectivity in the ventral semantic network is coupled with increased connectivity in the dorsal articulatory-phonological network.
source: In svPPA patients, recent fMRI evidence shows coupling of decreased connectivity in the ventral semantic network with increased connectivity in the dorsal articulatory-phonological one (Battistella et al., 2019; Montembeault et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Battistella et al., 2019 and Montembeault et al., 2019.

claim: svPPA has been linked with alpha and beta hypersynchrony in the left posterior superior temporal and adjacent parietal cortices.
source: Additionally, svPPA has been linked with specific spatiotemporal patterns of neuronal synchrony alterations: alpha and beta hypersynchrony in the left posterior superior temporal and adjacent parietal cortices, and delta-theta hypersynchrony in left posterior temporal/occipital cortices (Ranasinghe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ranasinghe et al., 2017.

claim: svPPA has been linked with delta-theta hypersynchrony in left posterior temporal/occipital cortices.
source: Additionally, svPPA has been linked with specific spatiotemporal patterns of neuronal synchrony alterations: alpha and beta hypersynchrony in the left posterior superior temporal and adjacent parietal cortices, and delta-theta hypersynchrony in left posterior temporal/occipital cortices (Ranasinghe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ranasinghe et al., 2017.

claim: During reading, svPPA patients can imperfectly compensate for their damage to the ventral route by over-recruiting the dorsal one.
source: Our findings also align with the recent observation that, during reading, svPPA patients can (imperfectly) compensate for their damage to the ventral route by over-recruiting the dorsal one (Borghesani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Borghesani et al., 2020.

claim: Neurodegeneration forces the reorganization of the interplay between ventral and dorsal language networks.
source: The present findings corroborate thus the idea that neurodegeneration forces the reorganization of the interplay between ventral and dorsal language networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior research.

claim: The task allowed engagement of semantic processing in patients in which the semantic system is compromised.
source: Critically, the present functional neuroimaging results and their interpretation rest on the fact that the task allowed engagement of semantic processing in patients in which the semantic system is, by definition, compromised.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data showing preserved performance.

claim: Probing the semantic system at the proper level of difficulty avoids the challenging interpretation of activation maps associated with failure to perform a task.
source: Hence, probing the semantic system at the proper level of difficulty (Wilson et al., 2018), we avoided the challenging interpretation of activation maps associated with failure to perform a task (Price et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wilson et al., 2018 and Price et al., 2006.

claim: Failing to detect a difference in performance does not necessarily correspond to similar underlying neurocognitive resources.
source: Our findings thus call for caution when evaluating studies comparing clinical cohorts based solely on behavioral data: failing to detect a difference in performance does not necessarily correspond to similar underlying neurocognitive resources.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dissociation between behavioral and neural findings.

claim: The sample size is relatively small, owing to the rareness of svPPA.
source: First, even if ours is the to-date largest cohort of svPPA patients assessed with task-based functional neuroimaging, our sample size is relatively small, owing to the rareness of the disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's limitations.

claim: Limited statistical power prevents further exploration of brain-behavior correlations.
source: We thus have limited statistical power, preventing us from, for instance, further exploring brain-behavior correlations.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's limitations.

claim: The subjects are older than those reported in previous studies on semantic categorization.
source: Second, our subjects (both HC and patients) are older than those reported in previous studies on semantic categorization, cautioning against direct comparisons.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's limitations and generalizability.

claim: The neural dynamics of visual processing are affected by aging.
source: While it has been shown that the neural dynamics of visual processing are affected by aging, the reduced and delayed activity observed does not necessarily relate to poorer performance, but rather may be mediated by task difficulty (Bruffaerts et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bruffaerts et al., 2019.

claim: Reduced and delayed activity in aging does not necessarily relate to poorer performance, but rather may be mediated by task difficulty.
source: While it has been shown that the neural dynamics of visual processing are affected by aging, the reduced and delayed activity observed does not necessarily relate to poorer performance, but rather may be mediated by task difficulty (Bruffaerts et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bruffaerts et al., 2019.

claim: Semantic processing remains intact during aging, but its neurofunctional organization undergoes changes.
source: Moreover, previous evidence suggests that even if semantic processing remains intact during aging, its neurofunctional organization undergoes changes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about aging and cognition.

claim: During a verbal semantic categorization task, older adults exhibited behavioral performance equivalent to that of young adults, but showed less activation of the left inferior parietal cortex and more activation of bilateral temporal cortex.
source: For instance, Lacombe et al., 2015 found that, during a verbal semantic categorization task, older adults exhibited behavioral performance equivalent to that of young adults, but showed less activation of the left inferior parietal cortex and more activation of bilateral temporal cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lacombe et al., 2015.

claim: The task design does not allow further investigation of potential categorical effects.
source: Finally, our task design does not allow further investigation of potential categorical effects.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's limitations.

claim: svPPA patients usually do not present categorical dissociations.
source: Contrary to patients with damage to the vOT due to stroke or herpes simplex encephalitis, svPPA patients usually do not present categorical dissociations (Moss et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moss et al., 2005.

claim: Category-specific deficits might arise from lacunar rather than generalized impairment of graded representations.
source: However, deeper investigations of time-resolved neural activity in svPPA could shed light onto the debate on the nature of ATL representations: category-specific deficits might arise from lacunar (rather than generalized) impairment of graded representations (Lambon Ralph et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lambon Ralph et al., 2007 and represents a theoretical speculation.

claim: The field lacks proper strategies to deal with tissue undergoing neurodegeneration while attempting to source-localize electrophysiological effects.
source: To date, the field lacks proper strategies to deal with tissue undergoing neurodegeneration while attempting to source-localize electrophysiological effects.
evidence: This is a statement about current methodological limitations in the field.

claim: The underlying issue of how tissue undergoing neurodegeneration affects source modeling is an open problem that requires further exploration.
source: Clearly, the underlying issue of how tissue undergoing neurodegeneration affects source modeling is an open problem that requires further exploration.
evidence: This is a statement about current methodological limitations.

claim: The interpretation of higher low gamma as a sign of compensation is speculative.
source: Finally, our interpretation of higher low gamma as a sign of compensation is speculative and lies on twofold inference: that more low-gamma band in svPPA means more activity, and that more activity means compensation.
evidence: This is explicitly acknowledged as speculation by the authors.

claim: In healthy and pathological aging, higher activation can be associated with compensatory effects or reflect neuropathology.
source: Previous literature in healthy and pathological aging suggests that higher activation can be associated with compensatory effects or reflect neuropathology (e.g., Elman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Elman et al., 2014.

claim: When considering progressive phenomena such as neurodegeneration, hyper- and hypoactivations might reflect different stages of disease and their relation to behavioral performance might follow a nonlinear U-shaped trajectory.
source: Critically, when considering progressive phenomena such as neurodegeneration, one has to acknowledge that hyper- and hypoactivations might reflect different stages of disease and that their relation to behavioral performance might follow a nonlinear U-shaped trajectory (e.g., Gregory et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gregory et al., 2017.

claim: Greater activity can be interpreted as compensation if there is evidence of a 'supply-demand gap' and evidence of a beneficial effect on cognitive performance.
source: Following Cabeza et al., 2018, we believe that greater activity can be interpreted as compensation if two criteria are met: (1) there has to be evidence of a 'supply-demand gap' and (2) there has to be evidence of a beneficial effect on cognitive performance.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cabeza et al., 2018.

claim: svPPA patients present insufficient neural resources (relatively focal ATL atrophy) and suffer from its behavioral consequences (pervasive semantic loss).
source: Our data clearly fulfills the first criterion as svPPA patients present insufficient neural resources (i.e., relatively focal ATL atrophy) and suffer from its behavioral consequences (i.e., pervasive semantic loss).
evidence: This is supported by the VBM data and neuropsychological profile.

claim: svPPA patients are able to perform the task with both accuracy and reaction times comparable with the HC.
source: Our findings also fulfill the second criterion as svPPA patients are able to perform the task with both accuracy and reaction times comparable with the HC.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data.

claim: The neural and behavioral evidence rules out alternatives to compensation such as inefficiency or pathology.
source: Thus, we believe that the neural and behavioral evidence we provide is enough to rule out alternatives to compensation such as inefficiency or pathology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results.

claim: Faulty semantic representations following ATL damage can be partially circumvented by additional processing in relatively spared occipital and dorsal stream regions.
source: Combining task-based MEG imaging and a neuropsychological model, we provide novel evidence that faulty semantic representations following ATL damage can be partially circumvented by additional processing in relatively spared occipital and dorsal stream regions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by the MEG and behavioral data.

claim: The results inform current neurocognitive models of the semantics system by corroborating the idea that it relies on the dynamic interplay of distributed functional neural networks.
source: Our results thus inform current neurocognitive models of the semantics system by corroborating the idea that it relies on the dynamic interplay of distributed functional neural networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the broader significance of the findings.

claim: MEG imaging can be leveraged in clinical populations to study compensation mechanisms such as the recruitment of perilesional and distal cortical regions.
source: Moreover, we highlight how MEG imaging can be leveraged in clinical populations to study compensation mechanisms such as the recruitment of perilesional and distal cortical regions.
evidence: This is a claim about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Eighteen svPPA patients and 18 healthy age-matched controls were recruited through the UCSF Memory and Aging Center.
source: Eighteen svPPA patients (13 females, 66.9 ± 6.9 years of age) and 18 healthy age-matched controls (11 females, 71.3 ± 6.1 years of age) were recruited through the University of California San Francisco (UCSF) Memory and Aging Center (MAC).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: All subjects were native speakers and had no contraindications to MEG.
source: All subjects were native speakers and had no contraindications to MEG.
evidence: This is a description of inclusion criteria.

claim: Patients met currently published criteria as determined by a team of clinicians based on detailed medical history, comprehensive neurological and standardized neuropsychological and language evaluations.
source: Patients met currently published criteria as determined by a team of clinicians based on a detailed medical history, comprehensive neurological and standardized neuropsychological and language evaluations (Gorno-Tempini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of diagnostic procedures, supported by citation to Gorno-Tempini et al., 2011.

claim: Patients were required to score at least 15 out of 30 on the Mini-Mental Status Exam (MMSE).
source: Besides being diagnosed with svPPA, patients were required to score at least 15 out of 30 on the Mini-Mental Status Exam (MMSE; Folstein et al., 1975) and be otherwise sufficiently functional to be scanned.
evidence: This is a description of inclusion criteria.

claim: HC were required to have absence of any psychiatric symptoms or cognitive deficits (CDR = 0 and MMSE ≥28/30).
source: Inclusion criteria required the absence of any psychiatric symptoms or cognitive deficits (i.e., Clinical Dementia Rating – CDR = 0 and MMSE ≥28/30).
evidence: This is a description of inclusion criteria for controls.

claim: Stimuli consisted of 70 colored drawings: 36 belonging to the semantic category of living items and 34 belonging to the semantic category of nonliving items.
source: Stimuli consisted of 70 colored drawings: 36 belonging to the semantic category of living items (e.g., animals, plants) and 34 belonging to the semantic category of nonliving items (e.g., tools, furniture).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: A behavioral validation study was conducted on a separate group of 54 age-matched healthy subjects.
source: To validate the set of stimuli, a behavioral study was conducted on a separate group of 54 age-matched healthy subjects (31 women; 47 right-handed; age = 74.21 years ± 8.63; education = 15 years ± 2.02).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus validation procedure.

claim: For living items, the average percentage of agreement with the assigned category was 96.86% ± 4.07.
source: For living items, the average percentage of agreement with the assigned category was 96.86% ± 4.07, the lowest score was 75.93% for the item dinosaur.
evidence: This is data from the stimulus validation study.

claim: For nonliving items, the average percentage of agreement was 99.18% ± 1.20.
source: For nonliving items, the average percentage of agreement was 99.18% ± 1.20, the lowest score was 96.30% for the items pizza and hamburger.
evidence: This is data from the stimulus validation study.

claim: The rate of agreement was significantly higher for nonliving items than for living ones (p=0.002).
source: A two-tailed t-test revealed that the difference between the two categories was significant (p=0.002): the rate of agreement was higher for nonliving items than for living ones.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the stimulus validation study.

claim: Nonliving items were judged significantly more prototypical of their category than living ones (p=0.032).
source: Again, a two-tailed t-test revealed a significant difference between the two categories (p=0.032): nonliving items were judged more prototypical of their category than living ones.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the stimulus validation study.

claim: Nonliving items were judged significantly more familiar than living items (p<0.001).
source: Even in this case the difference between the two categories was significant (two-tailed t-test, p<0.001): nonliving items were judged more familiar.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the stimulus validation study.

claim: No significant difference in visual complexity between living and nonliving items emerged.
source: Images of the two categories were also compared in terms of visual complexity (calculated as Shannon entropy via the python package Scikit-Image, https://scikit-image.org/). No significant difference between living (3.04 ± 0.84) and nonliving (3.13 ± 0.96) items emerged.
evidence: This is a result from the stimulus characterization analysis.

claim: The only statistically significant differences between living and nonliving categories in psycholinguistic variables were imageability (p=0.03) and familiarity (p<0.001).
source: Consistent with our online questionnaire, the only statistically significant differences between the two categories were imageability (living: 613.19 ± 19.62, nonliving: 596.43.15 ± 28.08, p=0.03) and familiarity (living: 498.26 ± 69.32, nonliving: 547.96 ± 45.82, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a result from the psycholinguistic analysis of stimuli, also shown in Table 3.

claim: Subjects were instructed to classify the pictures as living or nonliving by pressing one of two response buttons with their dominant hand.
